Riotous
RY-ut-us
adjective
From riot, Old French riote, “dispute, debauchery, wanton excess” — not chiefly a mob but a life of unrestrained indulgence. In Luk 15:13 it renders the Greek asōtōs, from a- (not) and sōzō (to save): living unsavingly, spending what cannot be recovered.

Biblical Definition

Riotous in the KJV rarely means a mob in the street; it means a life of unbridled excess — eating, drinking, and spending without restraint or reckoning. Solomon binds the riotous to the table: “Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh” (Pro 23:20), and gives the reason in the next breath — “For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Pro 23:21). The picture is not a moment of scandal but a slow undressing: the man who will not govern his appetite is clothed at last in rags, and it is his own drowsy indulgence that stripped him. The Greek behind the word is more terrible still. When the prodigal “wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luk 15:13), Luke uses asōtōs — literally unsavingly, from the same root as the word for salvation. He lived in a way that saves nothing and recovers nothing; every coin, every hour, every faculty went out and none came back. That is the essence of riot: not merely pleasure, but expenditure that cannot be reclaimed. Peter shows the other edge of it: the heathen “think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you” (1Pe 4:4) — riot resents the sober man’s refusal to run along. Paul forbids it to the church without qualification: “Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness” (Rom 13:13). Yet the prodigal’s far country ends in a swine-trough, and there he came to himself, and rose, and went to his father — and the father ran.

Webster 1828 Definition

Given to unrestrained excess and dissipation; wasteful, luxurious, unbridled — living unsavingly, spending what cannot be recovered.

expand to see more

RIOTOUS, luxurious; wanton; given to excess in feasting or dissipation; wasteful.

From Old French riote, “debauchery, wanton excess”; the mob-sense is later and secondary.

The Greek asōtōs is a- (not) + sōzō (to save): living unsavingly, keeping nothing back.

The riotous eater and the winebibber come to poverty, and drowsiness clothes them with rags (Pro 23:20-21).

The prodigal wasted his substance with riotous living in a far country (Luk 15:13).

Key Scripture

Pro 23:21 — "For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags."

Luk 15:13 — "And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living."

1Pe 4:4 — "Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you:"

Rom 13:13 — "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying."

Modern Corruption

Live: the age has made riot a rite of passage and calls sober restraint a joyless thing — but riot is spending what can never be got back.

expand to see more

Our generation has made riot a rite of passage. The far country is now a stage of life to be got through rather than a sin to be fled, and the years a young man spends wasting his substance are indulged as experience, as finding himself, as something everyone does. Peter saw the mechanism plainly: the heathen think it strange that ye run not with them, and they speak evil of you. Riot is never content to be private; it wants company, and it punishes refusal with mockery, because the sober man’s existence is itself a rebuke. So the restraint Scripture commands is recast as joylessness, and the man who will not run is told he is missing his life. Solomon answers the mockery with an inventory: the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty, and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags. The far country always sends a bill, and it is always paid in the one currency a man cannot earn back.

The principle to recover is written in the Greek itself. Asōtōs is un-savingly — the prodigal lived in a manner that saved nothing. Not merely that he enjoyed himself, but that everything went out and nothing came back: his substance, his years, his strength, his father’s honour, all spent past recovery. That is the true horror of riot; it is not the pleasure but the irrecoverableness. And yet this word is set in the one parable where irrecoverableness meets grace. The son who could save nothing came to himself among the swine, and rose, and went to his father with a rehearsed speech about being no more worthy — and while he was yet a great way off his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him. The prodigal could not recover what he had spent. His father recovered him. That is the gospel, and it is why riot is a sin to be repented of and never a life to be admired.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means given to unrestrained excess — living unsavingly, spending past recovery.

expand to see more

Riotous — from Old French riote, “dispute, debauchery, wanton excess.”

The mob-sense is later; the KJV sense is unbridled indulgence and waste.

In Luk 15:13 it renders the Greek asōtōs, a- (not) + sōzō (to save).

To live riotously is to live unsavingly: nothing kept, nothing recovered.

Its wages are poverty, and drowsiness clothes the man with rags (Pro 23:21).

Usage

"Be not among winebibbers, among riotous eaters of flesh: the table has undone more men than the sword."

"The prodigal wasted his substance with riotous living — living unsavingly, keeping nothing back."

"They think it strange that ye run not with them: riot always resents the man who will not run."
